title: Julian K  Jarboe - Procedural Sound Design for Roguelikes
speaker: Julian K  Jarboe
description:
This talk is from the 2020 virtual Roguelike Celebration:
https://roguelike.club/event2020.html

Julian K. Jarboe is a writer and sound designer from Massachusetts. In this lightning talk they give a brief overview of procedural audio approaches for roguelike developers interested in adding soundtracks to their games, and sound design tips to make and keep it simple, beautiful, and interesting.

Find them on Twitter: https://twitter.com/JulianKJarboe
Julian's doc with extended resources: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1XVqqV1RhkN1QCvbSrmnDvosyujtNEQUCA0a2uvJ747M/edit

segments.text: Hello!
My name is Julian K. Jarboe and I'm a writer and sound designer and artist.
Sometimes, especially with personal projects, I'm all three at the same time.
I wouldn't recommend over-extending yourself creativity like this, even (and perhaps especially)
with unpaid passion projects, but I suppose if none of us had ever done that, none of
us would be here at a Roguelike Celebration.
I say this upfront because the topic of my lightning talk, Procedural Sound Design for
Roguelikes, might sound overly broad or obtusely technical, and I don't want to disappoint
you if you're here for something that it's not.
So, for clarity, I'm going to spend the next ten minutes focused on two inseparable aspects
of what matters most to me about this topic in conversation with this specific community:
You should be thoughtfully incorporating sound design into your games if you are not already.
If you think sound, including its absence, is not an important or meaningful part of
your game, I am sorry to tell you this, but you're mistaken.
You can do this even if you have a tin ear, an empty wallet, and a New Year's resolution
to reign in the scope creep on your projects.
Musical talent, fancy software, and infinite free time are certainly helpful, but you already
have the most essential qualities for good sound design: you understand that even simple,
common, and fairly abstract symbols can convey an enormous amount of information, and furthermore,
you are curious and like to tinker, probably perpetually nudging a bit outside of your
comfort zone.
Congrats!
Well, here are Julian's rules and tools for achieving some sound design in your Roguelike
as directed.
FIRST CONCEPT: YOU MUST BE HONEST AND KIND WITH YOURSELF ABOUT YOUR OWN SENSORY QUIRKS.
THEY ARE ASSETS, NOT LIMITATIONS, AND ARE PART OF YOUR STYLE AND VOICE.
For example, there is no such thing as “just putting on headphones.”
Here are ten different reasons someone might wear them:
To quiet the noise of the outside world around them.
To quiet the noise of the inside world in their mind.
To relax or fall asleep.
To wake up or exercise.
To achieve a particular mood or attitude.
To focus and work productively.
To feel focused and productive while doing nothing.
As an inward substitute for companionship.
As an inward substitute for personal space.
As an outward barrier to assert personal space (sometimes not even listening to anything
at all).
Some people are always going to turn a game’s sound off and listen to their own selections,
and that’s okay, but understand the different reasons people do listen, and try to make
your game something at least you would want to listen to.
FIVE THOUGHTS ABOUT PROCESS: It needs to feel accurate, not be accurate.
If you want that punch to sound like a punch, you're better off snapping celery in front
of a microphone than recording a boxing match.
"Procedural sound generation" can mean a lot of things.
Writing software to compose a sonata is no more or less legitimate than recording your
own burps into your phone, putting the burp files in one folder, and then closing your
eyes and pointing at the screen to pick one.
(Some will disagree with me about this and they are welcome to write their own slideshow.)
Collaging and mixing together pre-existing assets (that you have the right to use) until
you make them your own is a legitimate way to design.
Using something given away freely for you to use, for free, is not cheating.
Collaborating with others, including hiring someone else in a purely transactional exchange,
is also not cheating.
You don’t need to do it all yourself!
SECOND CONCEPT: THERE IS MORE TO SOUND DESIGN THAN JUST MUSIC AND SOUND EFFECTS, AND YOU
DON'T NECESSARILY NEED TO INCORPORATE EITHER OR BOTH OF THEM.
Atmospheric sound, for example, often defies either category, and can be quite simple,
subtle, and powerful.
The sounds of the player's environment while they are playing, including the sounds that
they make themselves, are ultimately part of their experience of the design.
Even if this seems like a hypothetical woo-woo exercise, it does matter.
What expectations and conditions is your game made for?
Consider (imagine) playing and listening to your game and design on a small ThinkPad and
a set of CVS earbuds and no mouse, on a cramped commuter train.
Now consider this again on a surround sound home entertainment system with a massive projection
screen and a leather recliner.
Now consider this again on a 4k monitor and higher-end headphones, decent mechanical keyboard,
decent Staples office chair, rented bedroom.
We already think about this with the more established conversation around accessibility
and num pads!
Same deal but for ears.
FIVE THOUGHTS ABOUT TECHNIQUE: Audio sprites exist, exactly the way visual
sprites do.
You can economically bundle and reuse a fairly small library of sounds and modify effects
on the fly.
"Don't mix in headphones," if you can help it, though "studio monitors" (really nice
speakers specially set up for mixing) can be a luxury item.
I actually have a set and still can't always use them because I don't have the physical
space in my apartment.
So, let's revisit this one: Mix in the best over-ear headphones you can afford or reasonably
borrow, but please don't mix in earbuds.
Pursue a basic grasp of frequency bands.
You don't need to be able to run a fancy mixer at a live rock show.
You will want to know what "noisy" and "muddy" means with a lot of overlapping audio and
that you can fix it without removing them.
Understand why MIDI has persisted as a technology.
It's great if you deeply understand how it works, but bare minimum, try to understand
why it's valuable.
(Related: there's a lot of audio in the public domain that is available in MIDI form, and
therefore very, very easy to make your own/adjust!)
You can't always control for consistent quality.
Luckily, it matters less in the overall design than consistent volume, which you can control.
THIRD CONCEPT: WHETHER YOU CALL IT YOUR GAME'S MARKET OR GENRE OR TONE OR VIBE OR BIG MOOD,
IT IS A PROMISE THAT YOU AS A DESIGNER ARE MAKING TO YOUR PLAYERS AND LISTENERS.
Here is part of a very adaptable worksheet I originally wrote for fiction podcast writers:
What does your genre setting sound like?
Write down whatever sonic associations you have with ideas about the this setting or
genre.
There are no wrong answers!
Review your list of sounds, and consider what it is that makes them feel like that genre.
Imagine that tomorrow morning, our real world sounded like all of, but only, the things
on your list.
Are there specific types of music, machines, animals, weather, and people that are present?
Why?
Are there specific types of music, machines, animals, weather, and people that are absent?
Why?
